title: One hundred and fifty doors
told: from the first book of Samuel

card.keepWhy: There’s a psalm for whatever you feel.

sources: 1 Samuel 16:11 (David keeps the sheep); 16:14-23 (an evil spirit troubled Saul; his servants propose a man skilful in playing the harp; “a son of Isai the Bethlehemite, skilful in playing … and the Lord is with him”; whenever the spirit was upon Saul, David took his harp and played, and Saul was refreshed). In the Douay-Rheims, 1 Kings 16.
2 Samuel 23:1 (David, “the excellent psalmist of Israel”). Hebrew Tehillim (praises); Greek psalmos (a song sung to a plucked string). Hebrew kinnor, a lyre.
Psalm 23:1 (22:1 in the Greek and Latin numbering): “The Lord is my shepherd; there is nothing I shall want” (Grail Psalter, used in Catholic liturgy).
Matthew 27:46 and Mark 15:34 (Jesus cries out Psalm 22:1, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”); Psalm 22:23-32 turns to praise. Luke 23:46 (Psalm 31:6).

Catechism of the Catholic Church 2585-2589 (the Psalms, the prayer of the assembly); General Instruction of the Liturgy of the Hours; General Instruction of the Roman Missal 61 (the responsorial psalm).

The kinnor is a lyre; the caption says “a lyre, a small harp”. Confirm.

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? is there a song you put on when you’re having a hard day?
options: then you already know what this story is about.
perfect. that’s exactly how this book works.
that’s okay. some of these songs are almost silent.

steps.line: Near Bethlehem, a shepherd boy named David spent long days in the hills with his father’s sheep, and a lyre, a small harp, to pass the time.
In the palace, King Saul was troubled. A dark spirit hung over him, and he could find no peace. His servants had an idea: music.

steps.q: The shepherd boy plays his harp for the troubled king. What do you guess happens?
o: Nothing changes; the king stays dark
The darkness lifts, each time he plays
steps.why: Each time. 1 Samuel says Saul was refreshed and the dark spirit left him, but it kept coming back. Years later, Saul hurled a spear at David while he played.

steps.line: So David came to the palace. Whenever the darkness came over Saul, David took his harp and played, and Saul was refreshed.
Tradition remembers David as Israel’s great singer. Many of the 150 Psalms carry his name: songs of joy, of anger, of fear, of thanks.
steps.label: a long tradition

steps.q: Some Psalms are angry or full of despair, not just happy. Why would a holy book keep those?
o: Nobody dared to edit them out
Honest prayer includes anger and fear
They were sung only at funerals
steps.why: Laments are the most common kind of psalm. Many readers take that as permission: you can bring what you actually feel.

steps.line: One of the most loved starts with a shepherd, like David once was: “The Lord is my shepherd; there is nothing I shall want.”

steps.q: David later told Saul what shepherding had taught him. What had he done for his sheep?
o: Fought off a lion and a bear
Walked them to Egypt in a famine
steps.why: 1 Samuel 17: when a lion or bear took a lamb, David went after it. So “the Lord is my shepherd” means a guardian who fights for you, not just a gentle herder.

steps.line: Today, the Church still prays the Psalms every day. A psalm is prayed at Mass, and monks, nuns and priests pray them through the hours of the day.
steps.label: today

steps.q: Monks pray the Psalms through the hours of the day. In St Benedict’s old plan, how long to pray all 150?
steps.why: Benedict’s Rule, about 1,500 years old, has monks pray all 150 every week. He noted that the early monks managed it in a single day.

say: here’s what i love. the psalms were the prayer book of jesus’s own people. on the cross he prayed one: “my God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” even then, he prayed in old words.
the church prays them every day, at mass and in the liturgy of the hours. one hundred and fifty psalms, a door for nearly every feeling. you don’t have to tidy the feeling first.

steps.q: Psalm 22 opens “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” and ends in praise. What does that shape suggest?
o: Feeling abandoned means faith is gone
Only a saint could pray like that
The cry of “why?” can itself be a prayer
steps.why: That psalm starts in the dark and ends in trust. Jesus prayed its first line on the cross.

today.say: today, name what you actually feel, in one word: glad, tired, angry, lost. there’s a psalm for it. you can read psalm 23 slowly, or just breathe with your word. if you pray, you can hand God that word, just as it is.
options: lovely. read it slowly, like a shepherd walking.
